title: George "Pops" Foster and Mugsy Spanier Interview, 1957-04-21

pages.label: 001_George "Pops" Foster and Mugsy Spanier Interview, 1957-04-21 Part 1

blocks.x: Pops Fost and Mugs Hispania April 21st 1957 Real One This last time we checked out Don't you drink anymore, Pops? No.

I'm gonna take my old whiskey when it's... I take one of those exact... Oh, you see? Checkup, checkup, everything, see? I got the massages and everything, because I know I... I got anything. But they take me to prison and stuff that's given me to take me off of whiskey for about 15 days. Then I told the doctor, I said, Doc, well, I said, after 15 days, he's writing. Stopping. He says, you live longer than we stop it. I said, well, I quit. What do you mean? I said, I quit. Just like that? I said, like that. I said, about a month later, I was in the hospital. I went up. I said, how are you? I said, I don't want to be a foster. He said, you still quit? I said, I quit. The wife will tell you, I had to wait with me. He said, yeah, he quit. He surprised me, he said. He's all right. He said, I was gonna drink a... I drink like I'm out here with you guys now, but I drink a whole lot of whiskey. I go to house parties, drink a whole lot of whiskey. Meet guys at night. But if I stay home, don't see nobody, no whiskey. Yeah. You just don't drink all. You drink it at parties too, Al. Sure. And I didn't drink it like you drank it. I said, I don't want nothing but whiskey in that. Well, that's too much. Well, that's why I used to drink it. I can't drink it that way. I drink it straight. No chasers or nothing. Well, you talk about those days, you know. You could sit down and picture yourself in those days. They were... Easter Sunday, man. Jesus. Easter Sunday. Easter Sunday in New Orleans was bigger than New Year's. New Year's wasn't much. No kidding. Because everybody went to church pretty much on New Year's night, you know. Everybody, all gamblers and hustlers, all New Year's night they went to church. But Easter Sunday after Lent, man, there's more picnics. Like you play a picnic at the Millenburg, like today, years ago, big picnic at Millenburg. One of the camps you mean? Yeah, out of Millenburg. We called it Millenburg, we called it Millenburg. They called it Millenburg, see. They called it Millenburg, but it's Millenburg. That's what we pronounce it, Millenburg. But they call it Millenburg, see. Go out at the lake in New Orleans. Right on the lake. They have little calves, you know. That little pavilion you dance on and you walk out in the lake, you see. Yeah, we were down there a couple weeks ago. Yeah. There's still a few of them left, you know. Yeah. Not very many, though. See, but did you go down the wild woods? No. Well I'm not sure. We went out, you know, around the lake there on the side. You see, you could drive around that lake. See, but when I was there you couldn't drive around that lake. See, because there wasn't that many automobiles out there. Most they had out there was, see, most of the rich people had automobiles, see. And they had the pretty horses, the carriages, see. Were those camps, were they white and colored and both out there? You see, they had one side where the colored had their place, the colored had some nice place for the-
Lodges have them and so on?

Yeah. Or people have them? Well, people, like you owned a big camp out there and they had a big dance floor and all. You rent that camp, see. I see. And sometimes they'd send your cook out there to cook your spaghetti and macadre and make your gumbo and stuff. See, like they had a big picnic like Sunday, but they out there all day Saturday cooking, getting that place with you.
Yeah.

See. Now when you go out Sunday, they used to buy the big kegs of beer, and they had the kegs of beer, and they had the kegs of beer, and they had the kegs of beer, and they had the very best wine you could drink. Now you don't wait on it, nobody waits on you. Just help yourself? Just wait on yourself. Just pitch till you win. They call it pitch till you win. What does that mean? Just drink as much as you want? Yeah, pitch till you win doesn't mean to eat until you get enough. We used to have that slang, man this- like me was on the road, bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo place where a woman could go to bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo till you win. But she just put food on there and you just eat till you're good enough. It wasn't such a thing as you order a meal and they give you a little plate. She just put the, man they have some of the biggest platters you ever see, man they load that baby with chicken, fried chicken or pork. Sometimes the dish has steaks here, has chicken here, they have pork here, see. And you just go in that picture till you win. That's been a good spread. How'd you get the beer out of those kegs? Well they had, see they didn't have those quills back in the back. They had the wooden spigot, and they take that, they knock that, put that thing on there and they knock with a hammer. Well that thing goes inside the barrel, you know. They knock and put that thing in there and it wouldn't spread it, you know your beer comes out of there, but that beer was cold. See they didn't have a place down the bottom of this barrel where that spigot was. Well you knock that hole out of there, see. Put that ice on, you put that spigot in and you get that axe, man. Boom, boom, it's going in.
So you went through a hole and threw the ice and then into the beer barrel.

Yeah. That's what you could do. So it came out of the bottom of the barrel. So you just drink glass and everything, there's some more than ten cups. Because people would, they didn't worry, sometimes they have one or two cups. You wait till the other folks finish drinking and you grab that cup. It's just like your cow's milk what they got now. All this chemical stuff that they're using. See I see they milk a cow and bring the milk right in and drink it.
That's the best way.

Back in those days, I was still living. You know how they talk about cows that had TB and all that stuff. See sons have ruined a lot of things. Now you take me. I never, I didn't, see I was a bottom baby because I was very sick. My mother was sick when I was born. See. That's why I don't have cremable meat, wheat today. And they had to have a special car for me to get that milk from me. Oh yeah? Yeah, a special car. Oh excuse. See that, that's one thing the doctors know back then. The special car, one car milk was too rich a young man.
Wait what? Please come on up. It says 305 or 307. Alright. Loxie is coming up. I wonder if he can get him, we can get him. Yeah, when he comes up we'll get himself.

Yeah so, yeah there was some, there was some beautiful days back in them days. Beautiful women, man. Oh. Yeah? And then there's Ray La Dixie. You had anything you want. And for years no band, you couldn't get a band out of New Orleans because it was too great.
Why would you leave?

Where are you going? Where are you going having fun like that? Obviously I didn't go home for three or four weeks. There'd be two or three girls on the block. And I used to, where I used to play at, I could look out the window the girls hustling, you know. And the clarinet player, Louie Nelson used to work down there with us too in the district. And I had a piece of chalk and I used to watch through this window how many tricks, every time she turned a trick, you know, she'd watch it come and throw it in the door and mount it on the wall. Hey, man. You know Bob Campbell.

Yeah, sure. How are you? How are you? How are you? How are you, man? All right. We have a few things, we're having a few things sent up, Sam. Would you like something? No, I just have my lunch, thanks. Some tea? No, I didn't. Nothing? Just have my lunch. Want a drink? No, I don't drink.
I used to sit there and watch them throw that pee out the window, you know.
Chalk it up.

So she couldn't tell, they couldn't tell Louie she had three tricks when she had five, you know, because I had it marked on the wall. And that was true. Right now I was telling about that the other night, and it got funny to me when I was telling it, you know, and I used to do that. And like I'd go to the toilet, see what's going on in the mission then, you don't go to the toilet, you didn't mind playing, because the more you play the more money you make, you know. And you don't get off and go to the toilet. Louie said, Louie played a little straight man, so I'll sit over there and play. But he'd sit over there and play to keep calling all his chicks in case they turn the trick while I'm gone, you know. They turn the tricks about a minute, man. The guy go in one door and before you know it, you see that pee coming out the door and then she get out there with her broom and stuff. They call it van van. Van van? Yeah, it's some kind of disinfectant. But it smells good.
We'll have to draw some other tricks, you know.

And man, she got out there with the broom and you see that man. I said, Louie, did you get them? Yeah. I said, well you had two. I went to the toilet, I stopped the toilet. See I couldn't go. Once I go in the cavalry, I had to stay in there.
And I said, Louie, did you get them?

Yeah. I said, Louie, did you get them? Yeah. I said, well you had two. I went to the toilet, I stopped the toilet. See I couldn't go. Once I go in the cavalry, I had to stay in there. Because the cops would chase me. Because I was underage, I ain't got no business down there. But my boys being a good family. You're supposed to be 21 to work there, huh? Yeah. See I could go on one side of the street, but the cops on this corner knowed me. See you had two cops here, two cops here, two cops over there, two cops over there. Each corner? Each corner? Yeah. Well these two cops know me, and these two cops know me. But when I go in there like to stay in there like to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want to want Each quarter? Two cops, yeah. Well these two cops normally, these two cops normally here. When I go in there, when I go in the stadium, like I want a sandwich or anything, I had to send out somebody. I had a little chick. Used to send me my food. And King Oliver and my brother, man, they boys hit me for a long time. Don't eat that, man. That woman's trying to trick you, man. She's going to poison you. See? He said, you know, if they fix it for you, if we, they just don't even hurt us. That's right, Willie. I said, man, they eat all the food, you can drink the milk. She can't put nothing in milk. They let me drink the milk and eat all that food for a long time. Tell Eddie Grocer, my boss, Foster, it's a nice food. She'll come in. I said, yeah. I said, but Joe didn't tell me. Don't eat it. My brother says, because a woman can fix something for you. I said, my daddy, I said, can a woman do you anything? If she put something in for me and you eat it, don't want to hurt you. He said, hell yeah, if she puts something in for you it'll kill me too. He said, what the hell are they doing to you, Joe? I said, they tell me you don't eat it. What you don't eat of that boy? What you eat of your food? From then on I used to eat my food. But that ought to have been going on for months, you know. Does he? Don't eat it. And all the guys, and all the guys, all the dude for that. Yeah, man. Do that, man. You know, I wouldn't want to tell your mother that you got sick on a woman giving something to eat on that man, and they ain't going to hurt us. They all eat it man, she sent me big steak, fried chicken and stuff, there's something to eat later, and I'd be looking at it. And they'll, I'll get you a hamburger, Joe, I'm going to go outside and get me two hamburgers. I said, well I've got steak and chicken, they'll send me there for me. Boy, it came out and he said to me, my brother, my brother laughed at it right now, he said to me, he was right in the window with him too, helping me. He sent me a bottle of milk and a bottle of whiskey. See, I have a 2.15 apartment.

Oh yeah? Well let's, let's, well you know, we can all join in. Yeah. How did you first start, Rosie? Well I started on Clark Street, Chicago, just when I was a kid going to school. Are you a, are you a Chicagoan? Yes, I'm born and raised in Chicago. I didn't know the north side. Everyone thinks I was raised in the south side, but I wasn't. It'd be right up south side. I used to live on the south side and I had music, Joe Alvarez. Who were the first people you heard on the south side? Joe Alvarez. Joe Alvarez. No, Joe Alvarez wasn't the first one. Jelly Roll and. Manuel. Dominic. Yeah, Manuel, you heard Manuel from you, Johnny. Yeah, I heard that. Manuel Perez was up there for Donny.
You heard Sugar? No, no, no. Did you hear Sugar Johnny? No. Freddie Kepler. Freddie Kepler, well Freddie Kepler and Joe, yeah.
Back at Fort Dominic.
Jimmy Noonan, he was up there.

Well, by this time were you already, I mean, were you a musician or were you just- Well, I was caught in between three things. Be a ball player, study medicine, or be a musician. And the music went out. I used to like to play. When did you first start to study? Or play? Play, a professional job. I was around 14 years old. When were you born, Lindsey? Chicago. When? Nineteen-six. Nineteen-six. Oh. All you guys look so young, I don't know how you're doing, really. Well, you're taking yourself. Huh? You're taking yourself. I hope I look as good as you do. It's amazing. But just like athletes, you know. Yeah. Have to be the shit. An athlete can go on forever if he takes care of himself, but he doesn't take care of himself. He's through. It's proven. Same way with musicians. Some folks can get away with it. Uh-huh. First set like the time, if it doesn't show up in your health, it shows up in your playing. Well that's the end. Some people can drink and get away with it. I can't.
But when it hit them, it hit them all at once. Yeah. It did. Change overnight. We'll see what happens.

How did you first start to be interested in music, Mike? Well, I got interested in music. I had one of those old fashioned patrols at home. I was always interested in jazz. You don't want me to go to the other thing. Go ahead. I want to teach stuff.
Come on, wait a minute.

I got some records. I bought some Jeanette records with Joe Alvarez. Oh yeah. So I was going on the south side, and I wanted to find out where Joe was working. At that time, he was working at the Dreamland. Yeah. 35th Estate. Yeah. One of them. He used to have Wednesday matinees. Oh yeah? So. I guess they didn't have any relish. They'd go down there every Wednesday afternoon. Mm-hmm. Sit on the bed. They'd let us sit. They'd sit up in the balcony and drink Coca-Cola. Oh, just move around. And then, I think after that, Joe went to California for a while. That's right. And he came back. He went to work at the Royal Garden. And I was down there all the time. I was down there pretty early night. Was he especially your favorite? And were you following him? Yes. Personally, like more than anybody else. Yeah. I followed him more than... That was your man. Yeah. I had a driving style, you know. Yeah. Well, I liked that. Yeah. But were you playing yourself by the style? Oh, yes. I was playing professionally then. You were playing professionally? Oh, yes. And I liked the way Joe used mute, you know. That's where I got that from. Just was second nature then. Well, how did you first... I mean, how did you first... Why did you... When you first started, what kind of a band did you yourself play with? The jazz band. The jazz band. The jazz band. Elmer Schovel was in the band, George Brunus. Oh, yeah? Oh, yeah. What band was this? It wasn't the name of a band. We worked at a place called the Blacks Palm Garden, West North Avenue in Chicago. What kind of tunes did you play? Beg your pardon? What kind of tunes did you play? We played all the standard tunes in the day then. We never played any pop tunes. It was all standard tunes, blues and all that. Oh, yeah? Oh, yeah. Homer Schovel, he was a good piano player. Yeah. He was the only one that could read in a band. Uh-huh. Then I later started studying, learned how to read. Because that helps you out. You have to learn how to read. Sometimes. That's the way it was out, man. Pickle and my brother was on his tune read. I was right. In the afternoon. Joe was going to be much faster than he did. I used to listen to Joe sit out on the curb stomp when he worked at the Dreamland. That's before the, before he worked at the Dreamland, he used to work at a place called the Peking. Yes. And that's a police station now, upstairs. Was that an after hours place? No. Regular club. Oh, yes. Well, that time they used to stay open. Nine o'clock, five, six, seven o'clock in the morning. Oh, yeah? And I'd sit out on the curb stomp and just listen to Joe. Because he wouldn't let me in there.
Uh-huh.

At Dreamland. How old were you then? About fourteen, thirteen, about fourteen. Did you know him by this time? Oh, yes. I knew him. You were speaking to him? Oh, yes. Sure. Was he nice to you? Very nice. Very nice. He thought it was wonderful that someone could try to play like him. Did you ever get together with him? Oh, yes. I was privileged to be one of the first white persons to sit in with Joe's band. Oh, yeah? Because he wouldn't let you sit in if you couldn't play. He didn't care who you were. Uh-huh. And they had such a good jazz band that they didn't want anyone sitting in there going to spoil the band. Yeah. Joe liked you or he didn't like you. He was a highly sensitive person too. Uh-huh. Did he ever like show you things or, I mean, kind of informally teach you or was it- No, just listening. Just listening. That's all. Absorbing. That's right. And, of course, you know, everyone was coming down to hear Joe, you know. He wasn't very popular, but one of the musicians he was. What were some of the other musicians who after you began to- Well, Brunus and Paul Mraz, Rapolda, Ben Pollack, and El Meshogo, we all used to go down near Joe. Uh-huh. And Steve Brown, a bass player. Uh-huh. We'd all go down, we'd get through working, we'd all go on the south side and stay out there about six, seven, eight o'clock in the morning. And then, you know, Joe, what, uh, I think- What was the name of that cafe across the street from the sunset? Royal Garden? No, Plantation. Plantation? Yeah. And Joe and Plantation, I used to have to go in there and say hello to him. And then Louie was working across the street- At the sunset? At the sunset. And after I'd see Joe, I'd have to go over and say hello to Louie, because Louie, he'd get angry. In the back of bed, so I- In other words, everybody was very friendly with each other at the start. Oh, yes, sure. And I used to, I had a big merman then. I'd open the cutout out about the Indiana Avenue and they'd say here he comes. It sounded like an airplane. I used to take Joe home, I'd get his papers for him. You used to drive him home? Oh, yes. Is that so? He used to hang in a pool room. He was a good pool shooter. Oh, yeah. I forget, I think it was 31st and Indiana, and he'd be in there whenever you wanted Joe in the afternoon, you'd find him in that pool room. You'd be shooting in the pool. Oh, if there was a baseball game, he'd be in the pool room. Yeah. But I remember that, I think Joe used to play at the White Sox ballpark. I'd find a pool and all the best to play out for somebody eating. Because I was going to make a training trip with the Giants, so my mother would let me. And I used to go to the White Sox ballpark and work out out there. And I didn't know who that. Joe was playing in the bleachers out there. And I'd hear this cornet and I'd be pitching and I couldn't concentrate on pitching. I was listening to the musical. So that ended my baseball. Were you playing ball then? Oh, yes, I was playing ball. I pitched for Chicago Furnamon. Oh, yeah? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. I pitched against Buck Weaver. Oh, yeah? Oh, yeah. You became also professional baseball player. Oh, yeah. My mother would let me make the trip to Florida or wherever the Giants were training then. Oh, for the class? Well, I'd go to school. Uh-huh. I was going to school, playing the cornet too. My sister at school knew I'd be working all night so I'd come in at 9.30 in the morning and I'd go a half a day to school, one day and then a full day the next, catch up on my sleep. Mm-hmm. They were very nice to be the sisters there. Got all my marks so I was all right. What kind of clubs were you playing? Oh, cabarets in those days. You know, this is a four piece band, a five piece band. I was fortunate though, we always had a five piece band. Worked every place on Clark Street, thrown out of more places when I first started to play. I was like, I'm going to go home. So, I sort of licked that. I put on long pants, trying to make myself be older. Because those days when you put on long pants, you were considered a man then. You all right, Pop? Yeah. I don't have my brother's pants, I don't have one bad. That's what I used to do. I'd take my brother's long pants out where they'd just let me in the dreamland. Then one night, Big Brownie used to be the doorman at the peak end there. See? He says, oh, go on upstairs. I'd never been in the peak end. So Joe, I'll be there. I just sat down all over myself with Coca-Cola. I didn't want to go home. When did you start to, when did you make your first record? First record I made was Bucktown Five. First record I ever made. Who was with you? The Bucktown Five? The Bucktown Five. The Lolly Defoe. Mel Stitzel. Marvin Saxby on the guitar. And uh, Die Carey on Trombone myself. I used to have those records. You used to have those records. Good records, too. I don't have them, though. Really? You used to have those records with the rhythm case? When you went to, uh, Myth? Mm-mm. I got a picture there with you. Where?

What's where? You used to write that myth. Well, you used to the only song I know in that band. What band is that? They call it the rhythm case. It's called the rhythm case? Yeah. Myth mode? Yeah. No, myth didn't make it. I'm a myth. I'm a myth. I'm a myth. I'm a myth. I'm a myth. I'm a myth.
I'm a myth.
I'm a myth. I'm a myth.
I'm a myth. I'm a myth. I'm a myth. I'm a myth. I'm a myth. Yeah. No, myth didn't make it. I don't know. It was, uh...

Well, the chordal rhythm came from the Memphis Ennis band. Like when they had roast beef tuxedo and tuxedo and said, you know, you ought to see myth. That was the biggest thing about Memphis is a myth. You know, I got it from the second line, send me the... I give it to myth. Myth said, this is the one he never did good. Let's see it. When did you make the music?

When did you make those records with Mackenzie Condon? That was a little later, huh? Uh-huh. I just made one record with Eddie and the... It was one record then? Yeah. Be some changes made, found a new baby. That's the only one I made. I didn't make sugar and all that. You mean you just made two sides? That's it? That's all. Yeah. Then later when I went to New York or I made two, I made some. The Blue Busters. And what was life like for a musician in Chicago in the 20s? Very good then. Everything. If you couldn't make any money then it was your fault. That was the best deal. Money was just flowing like water because it was during commission days, you know. And all the big gangsters would come down, listen to music, and they all liked jazz. I worked at a place called the Rex, 22nd Estate. It used to open at one o'clock in the morning. That's when I was playing, I was through school and all that. I'd get through one job and then go to the Rex and work there every night. From one to six, seven o'clock in the morning. We got twenty, twenty-five dollars a week. And we'd make around $250 a week tips. Is that something? Oh, sure. Who used to come in there? Oh, Capone and all the gangsters used to come in there. Was there ever any trouble? Was I ever in trouble? No. Was there ever any trouble? No. No trouble at all. Remember they went out there. It was a good time. Perfect gentleman. You had good times, didn't you? Is that so? First thing Capone is due, you come in a place where you give the band a couple hundred dollars. It all depends on how you feel. All you want to drink. They were all that late. Remember they'd come down to Friars Inn. I'd get on a list of New Orleans Rhythm Kings. They'd do the same thing down there. Those guys, they really used to make some money in tips. Gee. They had a great big steel case with a big lock on it. And then between the entertainers and the band, oh they'd split maybe three, four hundred dollars a piece a week. Is that something? Oh shit. And every time one of those entertainers would go around the tables, sing a song. If he didn't come back with two, three hundred dollars or something else. Then we got smart in the cellar. We'd go around the tables with him because we'd find out about him first and we didn't know him so well. We'd go around and make sure, just watch and see what they get. And I'd come back and tell the fellas. They don't put it all in there and tell them about it. If Mike Fritzel found that out, he'd fire them. So they had to be honest. When Kapoor came, did he come with girls or were they just a bunch of men usually? Oh yeah, there's entourage, you know, guarding all around them. There'd be girls. Because they all like girls. I imagine they made a lot of money too. Who was that guy that Kapoor killed on Valentine's Day? Whose gang was that? With Moran? That was Doug's Moran. Boy, they could never prove him. When he killed his six. The Valentine's Day Massacre. Yeah. The Kilo Sixth guy? Yeah. That was in Clark State, in the 20 hundreds, in the back of the garage. Did you ever see him? Who, Kapoor? Moran. Oh yeah. He used to come down to Fryer's Inn. They all used to come. Every place, it'd work widely, you'd see some of them there all the time. Different nights. What was Fryer's Inn? That was at Van Buren and Wabash, downstairs in the basement. Was it a big place? Oh yes. That's where the New Orleans Rhythm King got to start.

Chicago was the number one spot for musicians in the St. Louis. Chicago was St. Louis. They had both fun on in the St. Louis. But then they, and the general, they had St. Louis over. Then you go to the Beardstown, Beardstown, man. Quite a few spots. Used to take us there. Where was that? Illinois. Who had St. Louis sold up? John Rowland who? No, General Hogan as a gangster. Oh. And Danny Colbeck.
Which was always the best spot. Did you keep up your friendship with all the way through the years? Yes. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.
I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. You're a good friendship with Oliver through the years? Oh, yeah. Sure. Oh, it's good. Dean O'Bannon. In fact, I had a fight with Dean O'Bannon. That was the guy I was thinking of. Yeah. He was in our neighborhood. He was? Oh, yeah. But wasn't it his gang that got killed in Valentine's Day thing? Or was it Bugs Moran? I think it was Bugs Moran. Bugs Moran? Dean O'Bannon. We were playing ball and I was covering third. He slid right into me and down I went. Oh, yeah? So I got right up and started right after him. And we used to call him Gimpy, you know. Gimpy? Mm-hmm. Why? He had a little slight gimp in his walk. He started out as a Tribune truck driver. That's how he started out. And he was really tough. His sister would go out of the room where they have to watch the death so he would go up and steal the pennies out of that. He was just naturally just like Tribune was hardy. What happened to him? He got killed. Five- Five- Five- Five- Five- Five-

pages.label: 002_George "Pops" Foster and Mugsy Spanier Interview, 1957-04-21 Part 2

blocks.x: Pops, Faust and Muggsy, Spaniel, April 21st, 1957, Reel 2.

Oh, man, don't you call it a little caillou? You know, caillou, and credit all that's a common dog. Oh, yeah? You call it a caillou, man, you're really low. That's sort of like being a caillouse. Caillouse, yeah. Is that going on?
Yeah.
There's a number we play, man, coquette. Wow. Do you know what that is? Dama la coquette. That means easy. Really?
Yeah, coquette is clean. In Creole? Yeah. It's that song. It means pretty in French, coquette.
Pretty, nice, you know.
Petite. Dama la coquette. Dama la coquette.
Dama la coquette.
Yes, give me some stuff. Oh, yeah. Dama la coquette. Were you a, are you of Creole origin?

Well, my mother speaks seven different languages and I don't speak one good one. I didn't stay home. I tell you, I was a rat man. And I'm the oldest one that needed all of the language. My brother and sister got them and they stayed home. And I didn't all try to use them, you know what I mean? You were the only smart one. Yeah. I'd go home sometimes, I'd be home about every day before I could understand things. Mama was trying to ask me questions. Why does he drive some coffee to the team, son?

Yeah, I wouldn't mind a little cup of coffee. If you have an extra cup then. Sure. What do you want in it? Just a little sugar and cream. See, we had one of the first swing bands in Chicago, you know. Worked with Sig Meyer and some hands off. It was a good band. How big was the band? How much sugar do you want? One and a half, right? One, two, three, five, seven, ten pieces. Sig Meyer, he played the violin, he was the leader. It was a very good band. Was it a reading band arrangements and so on? Oh yes. You know I worked with old someone? Muggs? Wrath. That's it.
Who? Wrath. You know the guitar player? Oh, I didn't know that. Yeah, because he used to play with George. He used to play with a big, heavy-shaped guy. Oh, I didn't know that. He played a long bass.
I played with him in 1921. 1921 on the boat.

I didn't know that. I didn't know that. He had a big, heavy-shaped guy. I didn't know that. He played a long bass. I played with him in 1921. 1921 on the boat. I didn't know that. I didn't know that. He had Penico with him. He had Penico with him. He actually had Penico break his armband. 23, Penico had his armband out there. When you first did you know that? He played with him. He played with him in 1921. He played with him in 1921. He played with him in 1921. When did you first hear Tesh, Mark?

Oh, I knew Tesh in 1925. When I went to Jimmy McPartland and Bud Freeman. So when I left White City, grew up in Midway Gardens, I got a hold of Tesh and Jess. We really had a swinging band at that Midway. I was considered the best band in Chicago at that time. Midway. Is that so? Oh, yeah. We used to outdraw the Trianon. You know, the big name band. Oh, really? Oh, yeah. Whose band was that? It was just a house band. House band. Right. Was Midway out on the Midway? Out near there? That was in the 60th and the Cottage Grove. Uh-huh. It was one of Lloyd Wright's creations. Frank Lloyd Wright? Yeah. Is that so? Beautiful place. It was called San Suzy Park first. Is it still there now? No, it tore that down, I think, around 1932 and 1934. Parking lot now. All those beautiful statues and everything. They're all gone. I tried to get one. The statues were the only one to give me. Where were they? Around the outside? Oh, yeah. Beautiful place. Like Lloyd Wright can only do. Yeah. I worked there for about three years. Went from there, we took our band, went over to Triangle. Tess was in a band. Jess, myself, and George Lettany. From there we went to the Mary Garden Ballroom on the north side. From Mary Garden Ballroom. I went to work with Ray Miller at the college inn. I stayed down there for a while. And I went with Ted Lewis. That was a nice sentence. That's when I first saw you, you were playing with Ted Lewis. That's it.

You know the further thing? I know the Muslim, but I didn't see the Muslim. Who was with Ted Lewis? When there ain't a town, I'm going out of that town. Or when you were playing the Palace there, I was at the Rose, and I didn't never get a chance to see you. You were playing the Palace right across the street.
Did you know Muggsy from Chicago?
I know Muggsy, but I don't think Muggsy knows me. I know it of him, but I wouldn't know him if I see him.
Yeah, absolutely. See? I've heard of Pops for years, but I never did meet him either. Who did?
When did you first meet?
I don't remember.

I couldn't remember that either. I was trying to think. I don't know where it would. It has to be in Chicago. It had to be in Chicago. I got a strong idea. It was either at the apex or the other. Upstairs at the apex, I didn't know if it was there. I used to come over there and go downstairs to shoot crafts or something. Downstairs, you know, to gamble downstairs in Jim Newman. Yeah. Then I didn't even have another little job on 39th Street. Was it Cuisbro? Yeah. Somewhere around in there. Near there. I went back there trying to figure out the spot, man. I got a project there now. I'm trying to figure out the spot. It looked just like I went to North and looked for a real electric man. Couldn't even see the real electric man. I just didn't know it was a project.
Well, that project just starts on 39th Street now. Yeah. The place you think about was the Palais Royal. Was that it? 39th and Drone.
I was a little boy then too.
That's a long time ago.
Yeah, I was a little boy. Where were you? You little boy too. Oh, yeah. You were a little pioneer boy. Oh, yeah.
That place used to run quite a long time ago.

Yeah. You know, when you used to kill us, it wasn't liquor. We got the best of us back in the middle of the window. Was that bad for you? Well, I just fool around. You see, because you're screwed so much. Because you got to have a fresh one. And every new town you hit, you got to get a fresh piece. That goes on the book. That's beyond the leader. Man, soon you hit a town, man, it's the first thing you want, man.
Why is that? Why would you?

And if you missed, if you didn't get nothing outside, you'd come in and look the maids over. That's what I used to do. I don't know if they ever got to do. It's like when I had the old Seeds, man. I'd go walking around town and I wouldn't see nothing. They'd come in and make all the floors, man. Look at the maids, see how they look. Especially look at them and smile too much. I would have them bring me a drink or something down and a cup of tea or, you know. And you know, Pop reminds me of the old devil who went confession so many times, you know. The priest got to know her.

She used to confess the same sin over and over. same sin over and over. And the priest asked her one day, gee, now let's get together here now. How many times has this happened to you? She told her she was raped. And she said, now, how often has this happened to you? She says, oh, it happened a long time ago, but I'd just love to talk about it. It's fucked, see?

That's what I'm getting outside, man. I'll show you. I'll show you. Look over there. And my main scribe was trying to get in the town and stay there while trying to give me a place where Lally's got a nice house and shit. I don't care if she had a husband. I don't even care. Even that landlady, you get a free rent to clothes wash. She's a fool. I got to throw her in many places, too, man. Well, we go from here now.

When you were first started, were you studying music? Or who did you start thinking? No, I started out thinking first, then I started to study. Later? Oh, yeah. After I was playing professionally about two years, then I started to study. Because you couldn't play in bands. You couldn't go to a pit or anything with that if you couldn't read. Well, from Ray Miller, yeah, I went to Ted Lewis. That was a nice sentence. Eight years hardly. How many years? Eight years. Eight years. I don't know what a depression was. I was making $250 a week during the depression. Is that so? I took care of my whole family and I raised a family. Sure. That was good. I was making $250 a week during the Depression. Is that so? I took care of my whole family and I raised a family. Sure. That was good. That's great. After Ted Lewis I couldn't stand it any longer. I went with Benny Pollack. Benny Pollack wound up in the hospital. You know the doctor that operated me, Ockman Ochsner? He was just sitting around the finest surgeons in the world. Yes, he's a famous. Who's that? Ockman Ochsner. At Turo. No, he said he had his own Ockman Ochsner, a foundation hospital. Oh yeah? New hospital. One of the most modern equipment hospitals in the world.

What hospital did you go to New Orleans, to Turo? That's where you are. You remember Turo Infirmary? Yeah. That's where every night when you called your number I said Turo Infirmary. But I didn't know that was the hospital you see here. See, I didn't know you knew what I was talking about. I said sure. Are you calling you all wrong?

There's no answer. Well, Archie was president of the Cancer Society. Just name it. He was the head of it. He was a fabulous man. Wonderful man too. We've been friends ever since the operations. Where are you now? 39.
Where are you?

He was going to save my life. He did? Oh yeah, so did he. Normally he touched me. We had Elstram. About an hour from now. Well, I started out with a perforated Elstram. You made his Monsiglo? Obstruction of the bowel. Well, did you know anything about Elstram?
Back in the day, what did you call them? Right?

Well, I think he called them. He called them Ancestral. He knew about him. An obstruction. Veins collapsed. He had 16 transfusions. Low-ver pneumonia. They threw the book at you. Oh sure, I was unconscious for six weeks. No kidding. I was operating on it four times. I didn't even know it. Must have just been hanging on the vine then. Oh, I was. I had low-ver pneumonia too. I was unconscious for about 21 days. Didn't know my way from it. See, the first operation was going to be a good one. They couldn't even move me from the room. They brought the operating room right down to me because they moved me and had been gone. Was it in New Orleans? Yes. I worked two days at the Roosevelt Hotel. Woke up in the hospital. I don't know why I'm here. I don't either. How long did it take you to get over that? I recuperated 18 months. One of my greatest thrills of my life was when you came to New York with your band to Nick's. I was living in Washington, D.C. I came to New York just to hear you. George Zach was still on piano. You know, your first band. Man, that killed me. That was a band. That was a band. That's one of the greatest bands of all time for me. Really. Brunus and Kless. What was his band? Piano player among George Zach. Rode Kless. Rode Kless. That's right. Rode Kless. It was a tight. We used to rehearse like man. I'll tell you, I'd never heard a band like that until then. In person, you know. I'd never heard a band like that. Because that band, they didn't just play solos. You know, now you just hear solos. This band was working with ensembles, ensembles, ensembles.
That's what I don't like. That's music. And that's what I don't like. What? I don't like solos. A bass is a string.
I don't like solos either.

A string bass is a rhythm. Mugzi had the right idea. But you got to do it. Now they want you to do it. I just like to get back there and just play some rhythm and let the melody instruments out there play. Just play them some string rhythm and let them go.

My brother and dad would drive to New York just to hear a band or we can go back. Back to school. Well, we used to rehearse at least twice a week. We'd leave in rehearsal and the band sounded like it too. Well, it showed it too. So I would get an idea. We'd drop out of our own arrangements. They'd have to put them down. Solos records will sound good always. They still sound good and they'll sound good 50 years from now.
Well, it's supposed to be. You hear him on Mugzi's records overseas. All records. I hear records. I didn't know he had made it.
Is that so?

Kids say, come listen to some records. They ain't got some records for you listening. What you want to hear when you listen to Mugzi. And since the year, they got him. What a year. What a year you want to hear him. They got him. And they got him. I was in the band and everything. You know, they first went started that. Putting every man who you got on record in the band. All the Frenchman's team. That was great.
They're supposed to be the most perfectly recorded jazz band. They sure sound good.
Victor used to do most of the recording.
Yeah.

There was Victor. At the Bloomberg label. Yeah. Because I made a lot of things with the guys who used to sing. Ray McChancey? Yeah. Because they're all the junk band. Gene Feistino's played suitcase with us. Jack. Brunus.

Did you like Armstrong when you heard him? Oh, yes. But not as much as Oliver. No, not as much as Joe. He was a rough man. He was playing second chorus. He played beautiful. Joe broke him in and all. You know that part?

Yeah. They had the quartiers. They had the quartiers all brass band. They said all brass. In a little small place. You could hear people. There wasn't no mic. People here. So let me hear them chuckle. They're feet.
Played soft. Oh, sure. Man.

Two trumpets. Trombone. Clarinet. Clarinet. Drums. Bass. Drums and piano. No bass. Soft, man. And then two trumpets. You imagine a drummer. You imagine a drummer. You imagine a drummer. You blow your roof off. It was soft. You could hear. Joe used to put a handkerchief over his fingers, you know, so that Louie wouldn't know what guy

would break he was going to play. They had their breaks numbered, you know. Oh, yeah? Joe would tell them number two break. They'd go play together. Huh? They had their breaks numbered? Oh, sure. Is that so? I thought that Joe thought if he watched his fingers he'd be able to copy it. He never dreamed that you could hear it, you know. Oh, it was really funny those days. Yeah. It was really interesting, yeah. The first time I met Bruno Stoyle, he was playing on a tin trombone. One of those old nickel plate things. Bastion. Like a toy trombone. On a vowel. A trombone.
I know you had an old tin vowel, man. I know that baby little dad was all tied up with some strings holding together.
I have a picture of him playing the peck horns. Playing what? Peck horns. What's that? Alto. Alto. Oh, no.
One of them horns would go to-do-do, to-do-do, to-do-do, to the brass band. They hit to it. That's what Louie played in the reform school, you know.
Mm-hmm.

It was funny back then, the reform school. I should have been under that reform school. I used to go back there and help them guys sweep out that long hall so they could hit the rehearsal of the band. Did you play with that band? I tried to play bass drum. I tried everything back there with them. I'd do my dirt, man. Get up a little bit more and go back to Jones' home. Walk by that long walk, too. Where were you yesterday all day at Jones' home, what you was doing out there, sweeping up the rehearsal of the band, and call up there and ask you what you said all day. Well, I'm clear of that.
I used to like to play the brass band. I started out as a drummer recently.

Really? You know, all your best swing trumpet players, all your best trumpet players, that they fight, it doesn't care how much the horn they play when they play with the brass band, the old guys, the first thing they put on is bass drum.
Yeah.
Did they have brass bands in Chicago?

I played bass drum at St. Mary's Training School right outside of Chicago. They put you on that bass drum, huh? Then I went to snare drum, and then I was just fooling around with the cornet in school. Wasn't even just practicing in between, and first thing you know I was playing cornet with the band. And then I just stayed right there. Is that the way you first started, at school? Yeah. Was it high school? No, grammar school. Grammar school. Well, where did you sit in with, where was Joe playing when you first sat in? Well, I sat in with Joe was at the Royal Garden. And I played Dipper Mouth. And there's only one way to play Dipper Mouth, and that's the way Joe plays it. And if you don't play those three choruses the way Joe played it, it's just not the Dipper Mouth. That's right. So a lot of cornet players, they play it different. I think it's because they can't play it. That's it. It's like Snaggit. Yeah. Because I've heard Joe play Dipper Mouth, and like Louie's cornet chop series, there's only one way to play that, and that's the way Louie plays it. It's like Carnival of Venice. You play that, just as written. Yeah. It's like the other thing, Joe would play Snaggit. Yeah. The introduction of that West End blues, you know, that was Joe Ollipurs. Oh, I didn't know that. Oh yeah. Joe played that introduction. Really? Yeah. What is that song?

Yeah, I hear all those guys. I heard Joe play that a long time before Louie. The funny thing, you play with a different band, you know them things out of the go, but you play it so wrong with different bands, and then you forget how to play it right.

Yeah. Did Joe play open match music? Oh yeah. He did play open a lot, huh? Oh yeah. He didn't always use some. He used to take one of those. What kind of different mutes did he use usually? What was that? What kind of mutes did he use? Those little con mutes, you can't buy them anymore. You can't buy them anymore. What did they look like? They're little tiny mutes. They're one of those. I have one of those. Oh, you have one of those. I have one that Joe Ollipurs gave you when I was a kid. That's the one. You have it now with you? Yes. I'd like to see it. Yes. Is the band going to be playing tonight, or is it tonight off? No, we weren't tonight. Well, that's right. The most mutes that I have, Joe Ollipurs gave to me. Is that some? It's made a German nickel. And you've had it all these years? Yeah, well I have five more of them, but I still go back to this one. I don't know why. Is that some? I couldn't tell you why.
He had a kazooke, a big kazooke. He tied two of them together and had a blow and hold that kazooke. You know the kazooke where they blew the blow? Yes.
Sure.

And then there's a guy in Iowa they call Tony. He got a pattern on that thing, they put two of them kazookes together. Kazooke. Made some mutes out of it. Made some mutes out of it. Called them bomber mutes. But that one kazooke would give a whole different effect, man. It wasn't one, but Joe could hold that thing that one kazooke and get the dog on his effect.

I mean he used the kazoo as a mute? Yeah, just hold it, hold his hand. You see, Joe used everything. He used to use a glass. Glass? What do you think? You'd say a tin can? Tin can. They'd have derbies, you know, they'd put that derby and do that.
No metal derbies, they were hard derbies, you know.

Did each one have a little different effect? Oh yeah. Different sounds? Joe would play it. Joe would just get on one tune and keep on playing it and he'd just play it, play it, and you know, every chord should be different. He'd just keep that on playing. He had an iron lift, didn't he? Yeah. How long were those tunes usually? About the same length as what you're playing on, I'd say? And when, say, have you all been back and played a tune? No, they were a little bit longer then. A little longer?
Yeah, five, seven months.

Oh yeah? Sure, it was all ensemble too. All ensemble? Sure. There was no solos. Cornette would probably take a solo, or a cornet would take a solo. They were about the only two who used to take the solos.
Well, a cornet band at that time, you didn't take down the drier lift, but you didn't take down the whole chorus.
No, I did.

You take down the, the trombone player would be the only trumpet you take down the drier lift, and it ran up again. There was no, you got a chorus or I got a chorus. When you hit the, it hit the, it was just ensembles.

That's the kind of thing. That's the kind of thing. Well, that was that little band I had then. That's, you were doing that too? That was all ensemble. Well, there were solos. And street, street rhythm. There was background. That's right. All the time, things were happening. That's the street rhythm. See, with our band, when someone was taking a solo, there was something happening behind them. Yeah. Today, a fellow takes a solo, he's out there and left the along alone.

A 17-piece band, a 17-piece band. One guy blowing the other guy, stood up there holding the instrument. Doesn't make sense. Doesn't make sense. Doesn't make sense to me, I'll say that. You see, when I was in the Louis Russell band, I used to tell Russell, I'd say, man, you got ten of you, man. I'd say, one guy, I'd say, let's say, man, that's antique. I'd say, all right, well, it really, really, they found out why that wasn't antique.

How did all that solo business get started? I'll be darn fine, though. I don't know. I guess the public started demanding. When musicians get stars like that, everybody gets a star. I think they had to get a name.

I think Louis and Joe started that round there, because they played all them big numbers like Snaggit and- Yeah, they played the duets. Yeah. And one trumpet they wanted to play, they wanted to be outstanding by themselves. They had a guy they called Kid Punch. We saw him in New Orleans. Well everything he wanted to play, he wanted to make his endings like Louis. Oh, he's got power if he just knows his horn. He's still playing? He's got power if he just knows his horn. Sounds like power.
Oh yeah, we saw a punch coming. He's got the power. But he don't know his horn. You don't know him, huh? No. You know Guy Kelly? He sounds like- You remember Guy Kelly?

Yeah. Well look, if you see him, you see Guy Kelly, you see him. Look just like him for the world. Guy Kelly worked for him, brother. Yeah, I bought, I had to buy it at what it mean to Lorenzo Stoyle, bought, paid three dollars for a horn out of the pawn shop for a- We couldn't punch, he didn't have no horn. Then he made us mad, we were going to take the horn, but Jack Carey, much Carey's brother, stopped him from taking the horn. I had the hatchet to chop the horn in half. I was going to give Stoyle's his half and I was going to take the other half. You know, he was going to cut it right there. I was going to tell you, no, give me my half and I wasn't going to hatch it, man. Let me do some crazy things, man.
Well, that's some camera. Yeah.

You know that's something I ain't never want? There's two things I was promised. I always promised a typewriter and one of them things. And I don't know nothing about either one of them. I never said what Joe Glazer told Louie. Louie bought one of them, he was that one finger. My sister. Yeah. One, there you go. Joe said, that one damn finger gets you in trouble. That was one finger dead, man.
I got a letter he wrote home, man, to me.
I was sick. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I wasn't working with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, I was working on Clark Street. And I'd be down to New Orleans Rhythm Kings, Mike Frenzel, if they'd get off early, we'd go out to where Joe was working and sit around and listen. And by the fact, we started out originally as a cornet team. Oh, would you talk about that a little? I didn't know that. Well, sure. I was working at the Vista dance hall on 43rd Street three nights a week. Vytavec used to come out with me. I used to get five dollars a night, so we'd buy a couple of pints of gin. Vytavec would come out. How did you first get to know Vytavec? Through Eddie Condon. I think Eddie Condon brought him up at the Columbia dance hall when I was working on him. I stuck up with friendships. So we used to go down to places where Jimmy Noon was working on the Paradise. About when was this, Maxim? Around 1922. Around that time. And Vytavec, and I would sit in as a cornet team. I used to work at the rendezvous. That was in 1925. I'd work at White City. Get through with White City and go work in the rendezvous for one to six and more. Vytavec was in Charlie Strait's band. So Vicks would stay after he got through and we'd both play. So we'd have all breaks together. Like Louis and the other. Yeah. That's the first time I still have to do it in 1922.

He was working in Chicago on Charlie Strait. This was the winter of 22. He had a Peewee with him, a drum boy. He had a band at the Arcade in St. Louis on the Alice Street. Well, he was around 22. He was in Chicago. The winter of 22. No, he was in Chicago then.

22 of the winter. He was at the Arcade in 22. Because I'd run away with my first wife and I know I was in St. Louis. That's what I'm doing. Maybe you were in Chicago. I was in Chicago then. 22 of the winter.

He was at the Arcade in 22. Because I'd run away with my first wife and I know I was in St. Louis. Maybe you were there for a week. Yeah, possibly. Because I know he was working with Charlie Strait. Was he good by 1922? Was he?

He was really fooling around more with the piano. Wait a minute. I think it was 21. 21 because the year before I left my first wife. Because I played with the Trum Boy on, what's he called them? C Melody. C Melody. Yeah. Trum Boy. Bix was on piano then.
Bix played piano. And then Pee Wee. And I never know who he was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was.
He was.
He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was. He was.

He was. He was. He was. We used to have a good turn. Bidebeck. Were you pretty good friends? Oh yes. But you really didn't play the same way at all? No. Entirely different. Entirely different. He played his style. Now just to say you were kind of at that stage influenced by Oliver. Who was he influenced by? I couldn't tell you. I couldn't tell you. I couldn't tell you. Bidebeck just had his own individual style. Who you were in? Spider-Man. I couldn't tell you who Bidebeck was influenced by.
Who did he hear mostly? Well he heard all.
All the bands that used to come out from the world. It was on the boats.
I don't know the bands on the boat. I was a bad boy. He used to play a whole lot of horn in there. I wasn't even a ton. But he could really go over his horn. Called Dwayne Jackson around St. Louis.
Who was that white boy that he used to talk about down in the world? And Emmett Hardy. Yeah, that's who Bidebeck I think used to try to play like. Emmett Hardy. Yeah. Did you ever see Emmett Hardy?

No, I never did. There was another guy called Johnny Lolliver. Nobody knew nothing about him. He was a hell of a trumpet player. I heard of him. There was nobody. There was nobody. Did you know? Somebody played a whole lot of horn. He was running to go to Richard Times and his daddy owned a half of French Mophage. Hey George.
Hello, Bud D. Well, it was last week, man.
How's that? He came in the other door, you noticed.
I know. Many of them doing that door side. Any calls? No, four.
No calls? No, sir.
One was from Egypt, man. George, you and I are going to have it out.
He's throwing another party when I come to Boston, wait till I come there. George, he's throwing a party when he's throwing a party. He's throwing a party at his house.

He was quite a pure player then. He was? He was really influenced by the piano. Yes. Oh, that shows on his records. On his piano things. Did he write most of his tunes on the piano? Oh, yes. Those are all original. To me, on the piano. No one knows what he really amounted to for your life today. Yeah. No one knows. It might have been greater than him. They'd write about you with body pooped out. I think he'd probably have gone to the piano. You think so? I think so. He would have left his chorus completely. Well, he'd probably go to the classics and all. Thanks. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

pages.label: 003_George "Pops" Foster and Mugsy Spanier Interview, 1957-04-21 Part 3

blocks.x: Pops, Faust and Muggsy, Spanier, April 21st, 1957, reel three. Did you like the way he played? Oh, yes, I liked the way he played. Did you get together and play a lot together? Oh, yes, we played every night in Chicago. In various clubs? Oh, yes. No, there was a round roll. Oh, there are. Then we'd go out together. We'd go out the south side. And I'd probably go there. We'd sit in there together. I wouldn't care to go. Rap could really play some blues on guitar, couldn't he, Pop? Yeah, that's why I... How good a guitar player was there? Wonderful guitar player. Did he play guitar much with the band, too? No, never played with the band. Never played with the band, yeah? Just played for his own amusement. Just for his own, but he was really good. Wonderful. We used to hire a launch, you know, in Chicago. And he'd go, and they'd get through it to the Friars Inn. We'd hire a launch and go out on the lake. And he'd take the guitar. We'd shut the motor off on the launch, and then he'd sit there and play the guitar. And there's music over the water. Very good. Sounds better. Would you go to your room and make your calls? What is this? There's one guy supposed to call me at two o'clock. Nobody called? I told you that. Or maybe he had a call, but that guy had left a message there. Look. They're Mr. Ween in 309. Did anybody call me looking for me? Would you... Tape wasn't running before. Tell us how the Oliver Band used to dress. What? You dressed in a dress? They used to dress in tuxedo. Uh-huh. And, you know, with the wing collars and small bow ties. But they didn't wear brown shoes and white socks. They didn't? No, they wore white socks with black shoes. First time I saw a double o'clock with a tuxedo, a little tie, white socks and brown shoes. I thought I'd die. They were laughing. He thought he was all dressed up. That's right. You know, you still see it. Guys come on the job with colored socks and a suit. You know, they'll have checkered socks. Brown shoes though. Brown shoes.

Brown shoes. And the biggest thing that I've seen, we were in the Primal Theater, Louie come downstairs with his tails on, shirt and everything with the pants. And they're blowing his own dress around there. I said, this is where you go on stage. I said, where the hell is your pants? Go to the moon, what the hell you talking about, my brother? That's where you go.
